thread.title: Safe Routes program canceled 14 years after starting
thread.title_full: Safe Routes program canceled 14 years after starting

author: ohtadmin
title: Safe Routes program canceled 14 years after starting
text:
State transportation officials have canceled the Safe Routes to Schools project less than a month after authorizing it.
Town Administrator Ed Mello briefed the town council at its Nov. 3 meeting. The councilors at their previous meeting (Oct. 6) approved an outlay of $700,000 to hire Mill City Construction Inc. to undertake the project, which would have installed sidewalks and curbs in front of the library on North Road. The project also included construction of a hard-surfaced path, compliant with the U.S. Americans with Disabilities Act, between Melrose and Lawn schools.
The Rhode Island Department of Transportation subsequently authorized that approval, which was required to proceed. Mello was told the project must be completed before 2027.
“We were given deadlines,” he said. “The project was vetted through an RFP.”
Twenty-four days after the council endorsed the project, however, the agency said the agreement had expired. The town has been working for 14 years on this program.
“They informed us that it was an oversight by them,” Mello said. “We cannot move forward with that project. They have canceled the project. We would have to start from day one.”
The project is administered by the Federal Highway Administration through a programmtic agreement with the school district, RIDOT, the Rhode Island State Historic Preservation Office and the Narragansett Indian Tribe.
“That has been the most challenging part of the program all along,” Mello said. “To get that agreement in place. So, to start that over again would be a daunting task. … The reality is that the project has really been struggling to get moving. It’s really been struggling to get funded.”
The good news, Mello said, is that the engineering, design and proposal process already have been completed at no cost to taxpayers.
“It’s ready to go if there is another funding stream that should become available,” he said.
More good news, Mello added, is that the portion of sidewalks and curbs on North Road and Watson Avenue could be included in a future state-administered project.
The Safe Routes to School project was born from a best land-use plan approved by the town council in June 2008, which laid the framework for federal grants being received in both 2007 and ’10.
Jamestown, since 2010, has been working with Crossman Engineering and the Public Archaeological Lab “for much of this time designing and permitting this project through the Federal Highway Administration.” Excavation in the area was met with scrutiny from the Narragansett Indians due to the potential for buried artifacts, which led to coordination with the U.S. Advisory Council on Historic Preservation.
This project was given approval to move forward with “specific archaeological protocols, including monitoring during construction.” A similar caveat was required when the Jamestown Philomenian Library underwent its expansion in 2023.
— Tim Riel
